definition: Following the usual, widely accepted way of doing things instead of trying something new.
example: Instead of a conventional cake, the couple served a tall stack of pancakes at their wedding.
nuance: Conventional stresses fitting in with common practice today; traditional stresses continuity with customs handed down from the past.
prompt: A home cook is deciding how to prepare the family's holiday turkey.
options: She chose the conventional method and roasted the bird slowly in the oven.
Her conventional plan was to cook the turkey in a way no one had ever attempted.
The market was conventional, just a block away, so she bought the turkey there.
Cooks from many states gathered downtown for a conventional meeting about turkeys.
reasons: Oven roasting is the familiar, widely accepted way most families cook a holiday turkey.
A method nobody has tried before is unconventional, the reverse of the intended sense.
Being close and handy is what convenient means; this confuses two look-alike words.
A large gathering is a convention; the adjective describes customary practice, not a meeting.

practice.prompt: A student is choosing how to organize a science report.
options: The library was conventional to his house, so he walked there to do research.
He used a conventional layout, with an introduction, methods, results, and a conclusion.
His conventional report was printed in a spiral on one round sheet of paper.
He wrote in a conventional tone, as if chatting casually with a friend at lunch.
reasons: Being easy to reach is convenient; the word here has nothing to do with accepted practice.
This is the standard structure that most science reports are expected to follow.
A strange, one-of-a-kind format breaks from normal practice rather than following it.
A relaxed, chatty style is conversational, a look-alike word with a different meaning.
